learn.title: Green Hydrogen Production via Water Electrolysis
learn.intro: Green hydrogen produced using renewable electricity is key to decarbonizing heavy industry, transport, and power systems. Water electrolysis splits water into hydrogen and oxygen without emissions, offering a clean fuel alternative. Two main technologies—PEM and alkaline—differ in efficiency, cost, and scalability, shaping the future of sustainable hydrogen economies.
learn.c1_text: PEM (Proton Exchange Membrane) uses a solid polymer membrane and operates at higher current densities, making it compact and ideal for variable renewables like solar and wind. Alkaline electrolyzers use liquid potassium hydroxide and are cheaper but less flexible. Think of PEM as a high-performance sports car—fast and responsive—while alkaline is like a reliable truck—cost-effective but slower.
learn.c2_text: PEM systems achieve 60–70% efficiency, slightly higher than alkaline’s 55–65%. However, PEM relies on rare platinum catalysts, increasing costs. Alkaline systems scale more easily to large capacities and dominate today’s market. As renewable energy grows, PEM is gaining traction for smaller, modular plants due to its rapid response to fluctuating power supply.
learn.c3_text: India launched the National Green Hydrogen Mission with an investment of ₹19,744 crore (~$2.3 billion), targeting 5 MMT annual green hydrogen production by 2030. The goal includes setting up 100 hydrogen hubs and incentivizing domestic manufacturing. Both PEM and alkaline technologies will play roles, with pilot projects underway in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.
learn.stat1: IRENA estimates global green hydrogen could meet 12% of energy needs by 2050
learn.stat2: PEM electrolyzers can respond to grid changes within seconds
learn.stat3: Alkaline systems currently account for over 70% of global hydrogen production capacity
learn.stat4: India aims to export green hydrogen to countries like Japan and South Korea

learn.title: Wind Turbine Lifespan and Blade Recycling
learn.intro: Wind turbines typically last 20–25 years, but managing end-of-life blades poses a major challenge. With over 100 million tons of composite material expected to retire globally by 2050, recycling is critical. Innovative solutions are emerging to repurpose old blades into construction materials, helping sustain the wind industry’s environmental benefits.
learn.c1_text: Modern wind turbines operate for 20–25 years under harsh conditions—high winds, temperature swings, and constant rotation. Regular maintenance extends life, including gearbox lubrication, blade inspections, and sensor monitoring. Operators use predictive analytics to detect wear early, preventing costly breakdowns. It's like maintaining a car—timely service keeps everything running smoothly.
learn.c2_text: Turbine blades are made of fiberglass-reinforced composites that resist biodegradation. Traditionally, old blades ended up in landfills. Now, methods like mechanical shredding, pyrolysis, and chemical recycling recover fibers and resins. Some companies turn waste into cement feedstock or new building materials, turning liabilities into resources.
learn.c3_text: India ranks 4th globally in wind capacity with over 45 GW installed as of 2023. Most turbines were installed post-2010 and nearing mid-life. The government promotes circular economy models through incentives for blade recycling R&D. States like Tamil Nadu lead in both deployment and early efforts toward responsible decommissioning practices.
learn.stat1: Over 100 million tons of wind turbine blade waste expected globally by 2050
learn.stat2: Typical wind turbine lifespan ranges between 20 to 25 years
learn.stat3: India has over 45 GW of installed wind capacity as of 2023
learn.stat4: Recycled carbon fiber from blades reduces raw material demand by up to 30%

learn.title: India's EV Policy and PM e-DRIVE Scheme
learn.intro: Electric vehicles (EVs) are transforming India’s mobility landscape. Government initiatives like the PM e-DRIVE scheme and state-level policies aim to boost adoption, reduce emissions, and build charging infrastructure. Understanding these frameworks helps citizens, businesses, and investors navigate India’s fast-evolving electric vehicle ecosystem.
learn.c1_text: Launched in 2019, the Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Hybrid & Electric Vehicles (FAME) scheme supports EV purchases through subsidies. Phase II allocated ₹10,000 crore (~$1.2 billion) to encourage 700,000 e-2Ws and 50,000 e-4Ws. It also funds charging station development. Imagine buying a bike with half off—FAME makes clean transport affordable for everyday riders.
learn.c2_text: States like Delhi, Maharashtra, and Karnataka introduced additional benefits such as road tax waivers, registration fee exemptions, and dedicated EV budgets. For example, Delhi offers up to ₹1.5 lakh subsidy on e-cars. These complementary policies accelerate FAME’s impact, creating demand pull alongside supply-side support for manufacturers and consumers alike.
learn.c3_text: As of 2023, India has over 130,000 public EV charging points. Under FAME, plans include 40,000 DC fast chargers and 380,000 slower AC units by 2026. Smart cities like Pune and Ahmedabad are leading pilot programs integrating solar-powered stations. This infrastructure expansion addresses range anxiety and readies India for mass EV uptake.

learn.stat3: Over 130,000 public EV charging points available as of 2023

learn.title: Smart Grids and Advanced Metering Systems
learn.intro: Smart grids modernize electricity networks using digital communication and automation. They enable two-way energy flow, integrate renewables seamlessly, and empower consumers with real-time data. Advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) plays a crucial role by providing accurate billing, outage detection, and demand response capabilities essential for a resilient future grid.
learn.c1_text: Traditional grids send power one way—from centralized plants to homes. Smart grids allow bidirectional flows, letting rooftop solar owners sell excess power back. This mirrors how internet connections work—you upload and download simultaneously. Such flexibility enables better integration of intermittent sources like wind and solar while improving reliability during peak demand.
learn.c2_text: Advanced meters record usage every hour or even minute, sending data wirelessly to utilities. Unlike traditional meters read monthly, smart meters provide instant feedback. Users can monitor consumption patterns via apps, shift usage to off-peak hours, and save money. Utilities benefit too—detecting outages instantly and balancing supply-demand dynamically.
learn.c3_text: India launched the Smart Grid Mission in 2011, planning to install 250 million smart meters by 2025. As of 2023, over 100 million are operational. States like Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu lead deployments. Integration with renewable microgrids in rural areas enhances access and efficiency, aligning with India’s goal of 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.
